summary: Superconducting granular aluminum (grAl) resonators with quality factors up to $1.85 	imes 10^6$ exhibit anomalous positive frequency shifts with increasing temperature and readout power at $T < 200$ mK, contradicting standard Mattis–Bardeen and TLS predictions. The authors explain the temperature dependence via quasiparticles in a Josephson-junction network with spatially nonuniform superconducting gaps ($\delta\Delta_0 \sim h f_0$), but the observed dissipation remains unexplained by two orders of magnitude at low temperatures.
motivation: Understanding loss mechanisms in high-kinetic-inductance superconductors like grAl is essential for advancing their use in quantum circuits. The exceptional low-loss performance of these devices ($f_0/Q_i \sim 3$ kHz at base temperature) makes previously hidden anomalies visible, requiring theoretical clarification.
method: Seven lumped-element grAl resonators ($f_0 = 5.31$–$7.53$ GHz) with quality factors $Q_i \sim 10^6$ were measured across multiple cool-downs using standard cQED techniques. Temperature ($23$–$300$ mK) and readout power dependencies were characterized; high-energy events from cosmic rays were monitored to extract relaxation timescales. The frequency and loss data were fit against Mattis–Bardeen theory, TLS models, and a granular medium model accounting for gap distribution in the grain ensemble.
result: Frequency shifts reach $50$ kHz but are decoupled from dissipation: the measured linewidth is only $3$ kHz despite large reactive components. A quasiparticle model with $\delta\Delta_0/h = 1.4 f_0 \approx 10.5$ GHz and residual quasiparticle density $x_{qp}^{\text{res}} = 2 \times 10^{-5}$ explains the positive frequency shift and its temperature dependence, while high-power Kerr nonlinearity is $K_0/(2\pi) = -0.54$ Hz/photon, matching theoretical predictions of $0.5$–$5$ Hz/photon.
